summary:
Agniyo - One Fair Satellite Fire Record for Bangladesh
NASA’s 25-year fire record for Bangladesh is split across two sensor families - MODIS (from 2000) and VIIRS (from 2012) - that count fire detections differently and cannot be directly compared, leaving forest officers and emergency responders without a consistent picture of when and where burning occurs.
Agniyo solves this using a machine-learning model that converts MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent values for any upazila, district or protected area, producing a single harmonized fire record from 2000 to today with calibrated uncertainty bands. The model is validated against NASA’s independent MCD64A1 burned-area product and passes a blind test on 2026 data the model never saw.
Built on this record, Agniyo delivers a burning activity calendar, season-start dates, unusual-month alerts, and a bilingual (English and Bangla) safety card per alert - mapping hazards, water sources, road time to the nearest fire station, and real-time weather - so fire crews can plan before they go.
This matters now: NASA is ending Terra and Aqua operations in 2026–2027. Without harmonization, the transition will create an invisible break in every fire record globally.
details:
Agniyo - Project Details

What It Does and How It Works

Agniyo solves a 25-year data problem: NASA has tracked active fire hotspots across Bangladesh since 2000 using two sensor families - MODIS (Terra and Aqua satellites, from 2000) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, from 2012) - but these sensors count fire detections differently. The VIIRS/MODIS ratio ranges from 1.9× to 13.4× depending on the month, region, and time of day, making it impossible to compare or combine them directly. Fire managers have been unable to reliably answer “is burning this year unusual?” because there is no common unit of measure.

Agniyo works in three layered stages:

Stage 1 - Harmonization (Machine Learning). A gradient-boosted ML model trained on 321,966 NASA FIRMS detections from 2000–2026 across Bangladesh converts MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent values for any upazila, district or protected area. It was trained on 2013–2020 data, tested blind on 2021–2025, and passed a formal blind test on January–September 2026 - data the model had never seen - meeting all four pre-written criteria. The model outputs both a central estimate and a calibrated uncertainty band, so users always know the confidence level alongside the number.

Stage 2 - Pattern Analysis (Statistics). From the harmonized record, Agniyo computes a burning activity calendar for every administrative area in Bangladesh: a month-by-month grid from 2000 to today in one consistent unit. It identifies each area’s critical period (the weeks that hold most burning), season start date, and flags unusual months - months where current activity is abnormally high relative to the same period in 2019–2025. This turns a raw data stream into an actionable planning picture.

Stage 3 - Alert and Safety Card (Rules + Map Data). When the last 5 days of live VIIRS detections exceed the 95th percentile of comparable windows for that area and time of year (with at least 20 detections), Agniyo raises a ranked alert. Each alert automatically generates a bilingual safety card - in English and Bangla - structured for firefighting crews: mapped hazards within 1 km (fuel depots, LPG stores, chemical sites, power infrastructure), nearest permanent and seasonal water sources, estimated road travel time to the fire station, forest office and hospital (routed over the OpenStreetMap road network), and real-time heat index and wind warnings from NASA POWER weather data.

Benefits and Intended Impact

For fire managers and forest officers: For the first time, an officer in the Chittagong Hill Tracts - where 74% of all Bangladesh fire hotspots occur, 97% of them in March and April - can open one screen and see whether today’s burning is routine or genuinely unusual relative to the full 25-year record, in their own language.

For firefighting crews: The safety card gives crews structured hazard intelligence before they reach a fire site. It answers the questions that matter: What dangerous materials could be near this fire? How long will it take to get there by road? How far is the nearest water? Is it a hot or windy day? The card is designed to fit two SMS message segments in Bangla so it can be sent even where data connectivity is limited.

For the long term: NASA plans to end Terra satellite operations in early 2027 and Aqua around September 2027. Aqua’s overpass time has already drifted from 12:55 local time in 2003–2023 to 14:25 by 2026 - a full 90-minute shift that changes what fire activity the satellite sees. Without harmonization, the transition to VIIRS-only data will introduce an invisible break into every fire record globally. Agniyo demonstrates a validated, open-source method to bridge that gap for Bangladesh, and the approach is portable to any country with long MODIS and VIIRS records.

For researchers: The full harmonized record, model outputs, evaluation results, and release checks are open and reproducible. The notebook runs end-to-end on Kaggle and passes 24 automated release checks.

Tools, Languages, Hardware and Software

Layer

Technology

Frontend

React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4 - phone-first, English + Bangla, light + dark mode

Backend API

Python 3.13, FastAPI, Uvicorn, SQLite - deployed on Render

ML Model

XGBoost (gradient boosting), scikit-learn, PyTorch + timm (deep learning, industrial classifier)

Geospatial

Rasterio, Shapely, PyProj, GeoJSON, Parquet

Data

NASA FIRMS (321,966 detections), NASA POWER (daily weather for all 64 districts), NASA MCD64A1 burned area, OpenStreetMap (fire stations, hospitals, hazards, road network, water sources), AWS Terrain Tiles (elevation and slope), geoBoundaries (administrative boundaries), SentinelKilnDB (brick kilns)

Training Platform

Kaggle (GPU-enabled notebook environment)

Design

Figma (full component library, prototype flows at 390/768/1024px, copy deck in Bangla and English)

Validation

Block bootstrap, Mondrian conformal prediction, Spearman correlation, Poisson deviance

 

Creativity and Design Thinking

Several creative decisions set Agniyo apart from a standard data dashboard:

Proving it wrong first. The team started version 1 with five assumptions from news reports and papers. After downloading all 321,966 real fire detections, every one of those assumptions was tested against actual data. Three were dropped entirely: the Sundarbans had only 5 satellite detections in 26 years (fires there are invisible to every sensor); brick kilns were not causing false fire alerts; and NASA weather data could not predict a bad season in advance. Building on what the data actually showed - rather than what seemed plausible - is baked into every screen.

Designing for the person who goes to the fire. The safety card is ordered the way a crew needs it: danger first (hazards), then access (water, road time), then conditions (heat, wind). Every number carries its limit: “nearest mapped station”, “±27% for areas this size”, “planning aid, not proof”. The app never says “no hazard” - it says “none mapped”, because the OpenStreetMap data is incomplete and false reassurance is more dangerous than uncertainty.

Calibrated honesty. The model’s uncertainty bands were recalibrated using Mondrian conformal prediction so that the stated 80% ranges actually cover 80% of real values (before calibration they covered only 64% of fire cells). Accuracy is broken down by area size: the app tells users that 90% accuracy per year is only achievable for the largest areas, and that for 425 of Bangladesh’s 521 upazilas - those with under 10 detections a year - the number is essentially noise.

Alert design against alarm fatigue. The first alert rule flagged all 26 live alerts as “HIGH”. After redesign, the same live data produces 3 HIGH alerts, 1 watch, 17 check, and 5 “likely industrial heat (night only)”. Fewer but more credible alerts is a deliberate safety design choice.

Language-first. Every string in the app exists in both Bangla and English. Alert text is designed to fit two SMS segments in Bangla (~140 characters) so it remains usable in areas with poor data connectivity. The writing rules explicitly forbid the words “illegal”, “arson”, and “proof” - a satellite reading is not evidence of cause, and the app never implies otherwise.

Factors the Team Considered

  • What the official data can and cannot see: The Sundarbans fires of 2024 and 2025 were not detected by any satellite sensor. Building fires in Dhaka (Chawkbazar 2019, Bailey Road 2024) produced zero detections. The app does not claim to cover these.
  • The sensor end-of-life deadline: Terra and Aqua retirement in 2026–2027 is the reason harmonization is urgent now, not in five years.
  • Ground truth the team cannot provide: Safety cards need testing with real firefighting crews; the app cannot make that claim without a formal pilot study. A pilot protocol is written and ready.
  • What only the government can provide: The official fire-station list, the hazardous-chemical register, and Forest Department fire records are not in OpenStreetMap. The app shows what public data makes visible and flags everything as “mapped only.”
  • Data freshness: The app displays how old the latest satellite pass is. Data older than 6 hours is shown as stale. The alert pipeline is designed to run every 3 hours using NASA’s public feed with no API key required.
